Today, I’m open-sourcing /fuck-cancer, an AI skill that helps patients and caregivers navigate cancer diagnosis and treatment and advocate for themselves and their loved ones.

Here’s what patients and caregivers have told me since I shared my mom’s story:

“You have to be a huge patient advocate. Ask questions and push for answers, biopsies, and proper testing.”

“I need help navigating difficult conversations and advocating for myself.”

“The volume of doctors, documents, and insurance paperwork can quickly become overwhelming.”

I built the skill to help with these problems. It creates and updates a practical brief with five sections:

1. Patient and care-team information for easy reference during calls

2. What to do next, limited to three specific actions

3. What we know, separating confirmed facts from what remains unclear

4. Medical terms explained in plain English

5. A care log with recent updates and decisions

It builds this brief from documents, and context you provide. When research is needed, it uses trusted sources such as the National Cancer Institute and the ClinicalTrials gov API.

I use it with ChatGPT/Codex and Claude Code to prepare for conversations and research. It can save the brief locally as a Markdown file or update a shareable Google Doc so the whole family can work from the same information.

tweets.text:
How to build great evals — Part 9

The Eval Roadmap Problem 

Most evals fail because teams treat them as static artifacts while their users  expectations and behaviors have evolved.
 
Your evals need a roadmap that evolves with your product and actual usage patterns.

Take a financial research agent. Here is how use cases will evolve over time.

Early user: Summarize this 5-page earnings report.

3 weeks later: review the last 5 earnings reports and explain their growth story.

2 months later: Here are 15 filings, earnings transcripts and research reports. Build an investment thesis.

Eventually: Monitor my stock portfolio and tell send me alerts when something materially changes my thesis.

Each stage requires different capabilities and hence different evals.

Your evals should change with usage patterns:

short-context -> long-context
single-turn QA -> multi-turn
passage citations -> doc and line citations 
Simple QA -> complex synthesis
reactive chat -> proactive agent

If your evals are stuck in week 1 while users are in week 3, it will show in your product and churn metrics.

Here’s a practical way to build the roadmap:
1/ Map the dimensions along which usage will evolve (eg # turns, document size, tool use, autonomy, journey coverage).
2/ Prioritize the use cases and dimensions that matter most for your product.
3/ Talk to your users, mine production traces to look for shifts.
4/ Build P0 evals for the next stage of usage.
5/ Run the evals, find failure modes (remember the taxonomy from Part 3), and hill-climb (from part 6).

The goal is to stay ahead of usage patterns. PM 101.

Drop your questions and I will address in future posts.

Share this with your teammates who think your evals are perfect.

Good post on what the applied AI strategy looks like at scale. It’s clear that there’s a wide gap between the AI models and the underlying workflows of an enterprise, which leaves a ton of opportunity for applied AI companies.

“The world doesn’t just want raw models and agents; it wants problems resolved and outcomes achieved. The premium will sit with the companies that can diffuse this intelligence through every aspect of civilization, converting raw tokens into real world outcomes, transforming industries, and creating economies in the process.”

This requires understanding the context, driving the change management, having a harness that can route to various models, connecting to the critical business systems in that vertical, solving the UX challenges of connecting users to agents in the right way in a workflow, understanding the evals in the space, and so on.  

That’s a ton of value that goes beyond just the model intelligence itself. And there’s a window of opportunity right now to build the defining companies that can bring intelligence to the critical domains in an enterprise.

tweets.text:
How to build great evals — Part 9

The Eval Roadmap Problem 

Most evals fail because teams treat them as static artifacts while their users  expectations and behaviors have evolved.
 
Your evals need a roadmap that evolves with your product and actual usage patterns.

Take a financial research agent. Here is how use cases will evolve over time.

Early user: Summarize this 5-page earnings report.

3 weeks later: review the last 5 earnings reports and explain their growth story.

2 months later: Here are 15 filings, earnings transcripts and research reports. Build an investment thesis.

Eventually: Monitor my stock portfolio and tell send me alerts when something materially changes my thesis.

Each stage requires different capabilities and hence different evals.

Your evals should change with usage patterns:

short-context -> long-context
single-turn QA -> multi-turn
passage citations -> doc and line citations 
Simple QA -> complex synthesis
reactive chat -> proactive agent

If your evals are stuck in week 1 while users are in week 3, it will show in your product and churn metrics.

Here’s a practical way to build the roadmap:
1/ Map the dimensions along which usage will evolve (eg # turns, document size, tool use, autonomy, journey coverage).
2/ Prioritize the use cases and dimensions that matter most for your product.
3/ Talk to your users, mine production traces to look for shifts.
4/ Build P0 evals for the next stage of usage.
5/ Run the evals, find failure modes (remember the taxonomy from Part 3), and hill-climb (from part 6).

The goal is to stay ahead of usage patterns. PM 101.

Drop your questions and I will address in future posts.

Share this with your teammates who think your evals are perfect.

tweets.text:
How to build great evals - part 8.

The discriminatory property of evals.
A hill-climbing eval is useful when it can separate AI systems that are meaningfully different.

Imagine you run an eval on five AI systems:

A: 94
B: 93
C: 95
D: 94
E: 92

Now suppose you already know A and C are substantially better systems than D and E.

The eval is bad cos it doesn’t tell you that. It has low discriminatory power.

It’s like giving a fifth-grade math test to a group of PhDs - everyone aces it and  you’ve learned nothing about who is the smartest.

That doesn’t mean making evals arbitrarily hard. Then everyone fails and you’re not measuring what your systems are meant for.

The sweet spot for an eval is:
Realistic + difficult + sensitive to differences in capability.

Over time, your good evals will saturate as your harness and underlying models improve. What do you do then?

Drop your guesses in the comments.

Share this with your teammates.

tweets.text:
How to build great evals - part 7.

The Goldilocks principle for eval construction.

Your evals should measure at the level of the various jobs to be done, not just the final answer.

E.g. consider a financial analysis agent. It's ultimate output is a stock recommendation. The most common mistake I see is teams create a golden set of right answers and check if the agent recommended the "right” stock.

The problem here is that there are probably a bunch of meaningful jobs that happened before this recommendation. E.g.

1/ Understanding the client: their portfolio, risk tolerance, investment horizon, goals, constraints

2/ Gather evidence: latest data points on the different stock stocks, the sectors, macro environment, Fed policy, recent and upcoming news events

3/ Analyze the data: revenue growth, valuation guidance, growth projections and produce a narrower number of candidate stocks

4/ Make a recommendation: stock ticker name, bid/sell price, timeframe

Each of these is a stage and produces an intermittent output. Each of them can (and maybe should have) their own eval so you can diagnose issues.

If the final recommendation is wrong, a well designed eval set would tell you:
Client understanding : 92%,
Evidence extraction : 92%,
Data analysis: 70%
Recommendation: 75%

Now you know where to go dig. And you might go, man the data analysis step is too complex and I need to break it down into a set of jobs to be done, and construct eval sets for them.

Not too granular. Not too coarse. Just right.

How to build great evals - part 6

Hill climbing on evals is just a fancy way of saying: pick a dimension that matters and optimize for it.

This could be improving the quality of existing features based on your latest production data on high value user journeys, expanding to adjacent use cases, lowering cost or latency.

The actual work boils down to better harnesses and model selection through methods like prompt eng, context eng, memory, post training, deterministic old school code etc.

Your failure mode taxonomy (from part 3) is a good compass for where your product struggles and needs some love.

E.g. maybe tool calling failures are your most common problem. You dig in and notice you stuff 20 tools in context, when each task really only needs 3-5. hill climbing here involves context eng to give it the right tools at the right stage and iterate until you get it to good.

Or take the cost reduction goal..
I’ve written about how I advise launching your product with the best model first. Get the quality as high as you can. Once you know users love the experience, hill climb to get similar quality with a smaller, cheaper, faster model. Same methods - harness, models.

tweets.text:
How to build great evals - part 5

Stop dumbing down the results from your beautiful, complex eval suite into one single score. This often happens because some senior wants a simplified number to make decisions. Happened to us in the early days of Gemini.

And I see it happening with a lot of teams.

This is the tyranny of the average.
AI systems do not have a simple dimension of quality.

Imagine a model that goes from:
85% -> 89% on simple summarization
80% -> 85% on basic factual QA
70% -> 63% on complex financial analysis

A single score obscures the fact that the model got worse on your frontier use case.

The immediate reaction to this is to come up with a weighted score. The problem with this is that you have  created false, mathematical procession around a judgment call.

So what should you do?
- keep a prioritized list of your evals per the ladder we discussed in part 4 yesterday.
- get people who can look at the details and don’t look for abstracted simplicity.
- Understand all the critical eval results in depth, where they fail, where they shine and make a decision on whether your new AI system is better or worse for your users.

Next post tomorrow!

Drop your eval questions below and I will answer in future posts.

Share this with your teammates. And your managers who run from complexity.
tweets.summary_zh: 别再把复杂的评估结果简化成一个简单的分数了！这样做会让你看不到模型在不同方面的真实表现。比如，一个模型在简化总结上提高了分数，但在复杂金融分析上却恶化了。要认真分析各项评估的细节，找出模型的优缺点，这样才能更好地判断这个AI系统实际上对用户是好还是坏。大家有评估方面的问题可以留言，我会在之后的帖子中回答！记得分享给你的团队和那些害怕复杂性的经理哦。

How to build great evals - part 4

The reason enterprises struggle with building decent AI systems is the lack of an eval strategy.

You need a laddered eval strategy, for your unique use cases,
with multiple evals on the cost/realism spectrum.

Here are the key kinds of evals you need:

Hill-climb long evals : this pushes the frontier of your product and you need to continually refresh this to improve quality and expand your feature base.

Regression evals : Did we break the product of today while hill climbing?

Smoke test evals: safety and the absolute basics that just can’t go wrong. Not necessarily hard questions, but important to not get wrong. Eg product identity.

Launch evals: often close to an online test with real-ish traffic. Less control, but the most realistic.

More in tomorrow’s post! 

Share with your teammates who will benefit!

tweets.text:
Great post on what post training looks like for applied AI use-cases to bring down costs and improve accuracy on certain tasks. This will increasingly be an approach that companies that can get closer to the underlying workflow in an enterprise will take.

The key is that once you understand a domain well enough and have enough volume on a set of similar tasks, it can start to make sense to purpose design models just for that work.

“In post-training, we incentivized efficient tool use and reasoning through reward shaping, preferring trajectories that would reduce tokens consumed at inference-time given equivalent performance. This allowed us to co-optimize for both cost and quality, gaining significant performance while keeping cost stable.”

Now, this won’t make sense in every domain, as general purpose frontier closed or open models will be good enough out of the box -or necessary- for the work at hand. But once you have deep enough vertical expertise, and either the costs are too high to do at scale *or* you have a unique enough task type not being trained on otherwise, this will make a ton of sense. 

Very compelling value proposition for being an applied AI company, and awesome to see multiple paths to winning in the market right now.

tweets.text:
My last post on ambition struck a nerve. Got a bunch of DMs from founders asking the same thing: why does ambition matter so much to investors? Let me try to explain the math.

A couple of things have happened, right? Anthropic became the fastest company to go from zero to a trillion dollars in valuation, beating every revenue record you can think of. OpenAI did the same over a longer period. SpaceX went public at $1.77 trillion. And then the Cursor acquisition was the bellwether. You have a company going from zero to $60 billion in four years, returning so much DPI to its early funds that there's actual, meaningful dollar growth coming out. And we haven't even talked about OpenRouter and the IRR there.

So LPs are voting with their feet, giving money to these very, very large mega funds. Fund sizes have gotten way, way larger, and that almost justifies the behavior. When your fund is that big, each investment needs to be underwritten to an outcome that big. Small wins literally don't move the number.

So when those funds are evaluating deals, even a Series A, their underwriting needs to be: hey, does this company get to a trillion dollars? If they have that belief, the entry price almost doesn't matter. They're underwriting to a very large outcome and hoping the company kind of gets there. If you enter at 200, 300, 500, sometimes 1B, it really doesn't matter. Because that's how they return the fund.

Even a prominent investor at one of the most disciplined firms says this. It sucks to not be at Anthropic or one of these foundational model companies. The value is just too big.

So what's happened in venture is that the error of omission is just too fudging high. They can't not invest. When something has a little bit of heat, price almost doesn't matter, because they can't go back to their LPs and say, hey, we didn't get into one of the biggest outcomes. They have to be in it.

The error of omission is way, way worse than the error of admission. And then power law kind of takes care of itself.

This is why ambition matters SO much when you're pitching.

现在的情况是，像Anthropic和OpenAI这样的公司迅速提升市值，甚至达到一万亿的估值，这让投资者十分关注。大基金的规模越来越大，投资时需要考虑的结果也变得非常巨大。所以，当他们评估投资机会时，甚至很早期的阶段（比如A轮融资），他们心里都在想：这家公司未来能不能达到一万亿的市值？因为一旦相信了这个，他们就更不在意进场的价格，只想尽量参与到这些巨大的机会中来。

总而言之，投资者更怕错过这些潜在巨头带来的回报，所以在寻找投资项目时，雄心壮志显得特别重要。

tweets.text:
The best way to get good at evals - Part 3. 

Let’s talk failure modes taxonomy - that’s the first thing you should build once you have v1 of your evals.

Start with your production traces - study the last 500 or 1,000 interactions and look at the failures. Cluster them and name the clusters.

Get specific - “bad answer” isn’t a useful cluster name. 

Specific failures - wrong document retrieved / right document but irrelevant section / failed to ground to context and hallucinated /  failed to punt on answer and instead made stuff up / question ambiguous  and made poor assumptions rather than asking clarifying questions etc.

Those are very different problems.

Once you can name the failure precisely, you can build eval tests specifically designed to catch it.

You now have the bridge from evals to an improvement flywheel. More tomorrow…

tweets.text:
Hi!

Recapping some changes we have rolled out over the last couple of weeks that have further reduced the risk associated to potentially destructive actions being performed by Codex during its work. 

A few weeks ago, we started investigating a small number of reports where GPT-5.6 in Codex took destructive actions outside what the user asked for. The most serious pattern we found was a command meant to clean up temporary work that could instead delete the user files. This should obviously not happen. 

Here’s what we found:
- Codex sometimes creates temporary folders while working and cleans them up afterward. In rare cases, GPT-5.6 got that cleanup wrong. One pattern involved reusing a system environment variable like $HOME for temporary work. A malformed cleanup command could then point at the actual home directory instead of the temporary folder. 
- There were cases where the model tried to delete or overwrite a temporary path without checking what was already there.

We’ve added protections at several layers:
- Codex is now explicitly instructed to check deletion targets before acting, create fresh temporary directories, avoid repurposing system environment variables, prefer recoverable actions, and stop when the scope is unclear.
- We strengthened the execution checks that identify high-risk deletion commands and escalate them for review. If a command is rejected, the model is directed to take a safer approach.
- We made Full access harder to enable accidentally, added clearer warnings, and further restricted especially risky permission combinations.
- We updated Auto-review to better identify destructive actions.
- We built targeted evaluations that replay the failures we observed. We’re also adding reinforcement-learning tasks and graders focused on these risks, and filtering destructive actions from training data.

In those replay evaluations, the changes substantially reduced the behavior while preserving Codex’s ability to complete normal coding work. 

Two things to do on your end:
- Keep the Codex app up to date. We are always improving safety, performance and many other things.
- Use one of the sandbox modes: "Ask for approval" or "Approve for me". Only use Full access for environments you trust and can recover.

Thanks and happy Codexing out there!

Here’s how to think about the cost of your evals : treat evals like frontier models…establish the quality frontier first, then work your way down the cost curve.

Start with the highest quality way you can know if your AI product is working as intended.

First get clear on what good looks like - Write the rubric.

Then figure out the best way to measure it - humans /  LLM judge / automated verification.

At this stage, spend the money - use the expensive judge model, pay humans (or give your time). Run the best eval process possible so you get a signal you trust.

Once the eval can reliably distinguish good from bad and reflects what you care about in the product, focus on costs - more automation, smaller judge models, sampling, deterministic checks where relevant.

Quality first. Cost next.

tweets.text:
As we’re seeing in case study after case study, it turns out that the amount of value that can be created between the AI model and the ultimate end-user workflow is far larger than many people assumed or realized. 

Model capability is obviously doing a lot of heavy lifting in agentic products, but there’s still a lot more work to diffuse AI into the enterprise.

1. Getting agents to work well (and alongside people) in mission critical workflows tends to need to be represented differently depending on the business process. Sometimes it’s a chat experience. Other times it’s a background agent running in a deterministic workflow. And dozens of other variants. This is a mix of needing a harness that’s tuned to specific domains of work, but also making it show up in the right product experience.

2. Different workflows connect into entirely different enterprise systems and need access to very different data. Working with that data -whether it’s life sciences, financial, legal, etc.- requires contextual approaches, understanding of the data, having the right user experience for data interaction, and more.

3. The need for domain-specific change management remains critical in most verticals. The way you talk and implement technology at a bank is very different from a law firm. Having the right talent with a singular mission ends up being extremely useful for something as complex as process reengineering.

4. The ability to work with a variety of models means you can tune the workflows to different cost and performance levels. And you can eventually post train models for specific tasks to tailor the outcomes and eke out gains that aren’t coming otherwise in frontier models.

5. Evals! AI is basically not useful if it can’t be evaluated. Domain-specific evals that let you dramatically improve the performance of your harness for specific workflows just has a crazy long tail given how many tasks there are in the economy. Nearly impossible for one system to be tuned for all of them.

6. Lots of verticals and domains require pricing models that reflect relevant abstractions on top of tokens alone. The ability to price in ways that work for your industry’s consumption model ends up mattering in a variety of spaces. 

This just touches on some of the things that go into the applied AI layer. But it all adds up to being a huge surface area for being able to sustainably innovate and differentiate.

这个视频讲述了一种微型芯片的创新应用，这种芯片有可能治愈失明，帮助人们重见光明。通过技术的突破，这项发明展示了如何利用先进科技改善人类生活质量，并探讨了未来可能的医疗应用。

💡 值得一看 — 这个视频提供了关于前沿技术在医疗领域应用的洞察，可能为你在创意设计和品牌营销中带来启发。

podcasts.name: Fireship
podcasts.title: DeepSeek is back... and Silicon Valley is terrified
podcasts.summary_zh:
视频讨论了DeepSeek这一AI工具的回归以及它对硅谷的影响，引发了业内对AI技术发展的担忧。视频分析了DeepSeek的强大功能以及它可能改变创意产业和商业模式的潜力，反映出当前AI技术在市场竞争中的关键性。

🎯 推荐 Yves 观看 — 这个视频与Logic Labs在AI产品开发的趋势密切相关，同时也可以给TexTale在电商运营中利用创意工具的思路提供启示。

podcasts.name: Lenny's Podcast
podcasts.title: The One Trait that Matters Most in the AI Age
podcasts.summary_zh:
这个视频讨论了在人工智能时代最重要的特质，即适应能力和持续学习的能力。主持人探讨了如何在快速变化的科技环境中保持竞争力，以及人们如何可以利用这些特质来应对未来的挑战。

🎯 推荐 Yves 观看 — 适应能力在 AI 工具和产品开发中至关重要，而这正是你在 Logic Labs 和 TexTale 中推动创新所需要的关键技能。

podcasts.name: Matt Wolfe
podcasts.title: Parenting advice from Khabib: Lessons learned from his father | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
podcasts.summary_zh:
这段视频中，Khabib Nurmagomedov 分享了他父亲的教育理念和人生智慧，强调了责任、纪律和坚持的重要性。他的经历提供了一些关于如何在追求成功的过程中保持谦逊和坚韧的启示。

💡 值得一看 — Khabib 的教导不仅适用于运动员，也能为任何创业者提供宝贵的人生哲理，特别是在面对挑战和压力时。对于 Logic Labs 和 TexTale 的运营有启示意义。

podcasts.name: Data Driven NYC
podcasts.title: Why everyone at this $1B startup whispers into microphones #ai  #podcast
podcasts.summary_zh:
这个视频讨论了一家市值达到10亿美元的初创公司为何在团队中推广使用麦克风进行沟通的原因，强调这种方式如何提升创意过程和团队协作的效率。视频深入探讨了通过音频录入来收集创意、反馈和讨论的价值，尤其在AI和创新设计的环境下显得尤为重要。

🎯 推荐 Yves 观看 — 因为视频中的创意沟通方法与 Logic Labs 和 TexTale 的创意设计过程密切相关，可以为您在品牌营销中带来新的思路。

podcasts.name: Tiago Forte
podcasts.title: Nick Milo Reads My Obsidian Vault Like a Doctor
podcasts.summary_zh:
这个视频中，Nick Milo 深入解读了 Tiago Forte 的 Obsidian Vault，像医生一样分析其结构和内容，强调了如何高效利用笔记和资料管理工具来提升创造力和生产力。他分享了关于信息如何组织的重要性以及如何更好地引导思维的技巧。

🎯 推荐 Yves 观看 — 这个视频对 Logic Labs 在 AI 工具的开发和 TexTale 的创意设计工作非常有帮助，尤其是在信息管理和创意流程的优化方面。

podcasts.name: South Park Commons
podcasts.title: The Secret Superpower of Great Founders
podcasts.summary_zh:
这个视频探讨了伟大创始人背后的秘密超级能力，包括他们如何识别和利用自身优势，以及在面对挑战时的决策能力。通过讲述成功创业者的故事，视频为观众揭示了这些能力如何推动企业发展和创新。

🎯 推荐 Yves 观看 — 由于视频中的内容与创业者在AI行业中的决策能力直接相关，对于Logic Labs和TexTale的创意设计及运营有很大的启发作用。

podcasts.name: South Park Commons
podcasts.title: The Secret Superpower of Great Founders | Sridhar Ramaswamy (Snowflake CEO)
podcasts.summary_zh:
这段视频中，Snowflake CEO Sridhar Ramaswamy 分享了优秀创始人的“秘密超能力”，强调在创业过程中勇于创新和追求独特性的重要性。他讨论了成功公司如何利用数据驱动决策，提升产品和服务的质量，从而在竞争中脱颖而出。

🎯 推荐 Yves 观看 — 这个视频探讨了创新和数据驱动的重要性，与 Logic Labs 和 TexTale 的创业过程密切相关，能够激发你的创意设计灵感。

podcasts.name: Y Combinator
podcasts.title: Going In Deep On Data | YC Paper Club
podcasts.summary_zh:
这个视频探讨了数据的重要性以及如何在创业过程中有效利用数据进行决策。嘉宾分享了在Y Combinator支持的初创企业中关于数据驱动决策的最佳实践，特别是如何通过数据分析来优化产品和市场策略。

🎯 推荐 Yves 观看 — 这个视频为Logic Labs和TexTale提供了关于数据在创意设计和电商运营中的应用见解，能助力你更好地理解如何利用数据驱动品牌决策。

podcasts.name: No Priors
podcasts.title: From Restoring Sight to Reimagining the Brain, with Max Hodak
podcasts.summary_zh:
本视频邀请了 Max Hodak，他是一位在恢复视觉和重新想象大脑方面做出创新的人士。他分享了将科技与人类认知结合的想法，并探讨了如何利用人工智能为各个领域带来变革。

💡 值得一看 — Max Hodak 的观点将为你提供关于科技与人类认知结合的新视角，可能对你在 Logic Labs 和 TexTale 的创意设计有启发。

podcasts.name: Matt Wolfe
podcasts.title: Khabib explains warrior culture of Dagestan | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
podcasts.summary_zh:
这段视频中，著名 MMA 选手哈比布·努尔马戈梅多夫与莱克斯·弗里德曼探讨了达吉斯坦的武士文化。哈比布分享了他在这种文化背景下成长的经历，以及这种文化对他作为运动员和领袖的影响，凸显了传统价值观和精神的重要性。

💡 值得一看 — 视频中关于文化与价值观的探讨，可以激发 Yves 在创意设计和品牌营销中的思考，尤其是如何将传统文化融入现代科技服装中的设计理念。

podcasts.name: Lenny's Podcast
podcasts.title: Why This is the Best Time to be a Designer
podcasts.summary_zh:
这个视频探讨了当今设计师面临的前所未有的机会，强调了技术进步和创意工具的结合如何赋予设计师更多的自由和影响力。主持人分享了不断变化的设计环境，以及如何利用AI和其他新兴技术来提升设计过程。

🎯 推荐 Yves 观看 — 这个视频能为你在Logic Labs和TexTale的创意设计提供灵感，帮助你理解如何利用当前趋势和工具提升品牌和产品的竞争力。

producthunt.name: Prelint
producthunt.tagline: Prevent product drift in AI-written code
producthunt.summary_zh: Prelint 是一款专为 AI 编写的代码设计的工具，旨在防止代码偏离预期标准。它能够实时检测和修正代码中的问题，确保代码质量和一致性。通过使用 Prelint，可以提高代码的可靠性和可维护性。

producthunt.name: Hey Noah
producthunt.tagline: A proactive AI executive assistant for founders
producthunt.summary_zh: Hey Noah是一款主动智能助手，专为创始人设计。它能够管理日程安排、处理邮件和提供业务建议，让用户更高效地专注于公司的发展。通过AI技术，Hey Noah帮助用户简化日常管理任务。

producthunt.name: AdAnt AI
producthunt.tagline: Claude for viral, high-converting social ads
producthunt.summary_zh: AdAnt AI 是一款基于人工智能的工具，专门用于创建具有病毒传播性和高转化率的社交广告。它能够快速生成吸引人的广告文案和创意，帮助用户在社交媒体上提高曝光率和销售转化。简单易用，适合希望优化广告效果的用户。

producthunt.name: SKI
producthunt.tagline: Free voice coding for Claude Code, Codex and more
producthunt.summary_zh: SKI是一款免费语音编程工具，支持Claude Code、Codex等多种编程语言。用户可以通过语音输入代码，简化编程过程，提高效率。该产品旨在让编程变得更便捷。

producthunt.name: Clipto MCP
producthunt.tagline: Let agents source clips from terabytes of your local video
producthunt.summary_zh: Clipto MCP 是一款视频剪辑工具，允许用户从本地海量视频中快速提取片段。它支持高效整理和查找视频素材，方便用户在创作中使用。

producthunt.name: Prefactor
producthunt.tagline: Evaluate your AI Agents in real-time
producthunt.summary_zh: Prefactor是一个实时评估AI代理的工具。它能够帮助用户监测和分析AI代理的表现，让用户更好地理解其工作效果。通过这个工具，用户可以即时获取反馈，优化AI代理的使用。

producthunt.name: Wispr Flow Notetaker
producthunt.tagline: Meeting notes that get the details right.
producthunt.summary_zh: Wispr Flow Notetaker是一款会议记录工具，能够自动整理和记录会议内容。它精准捕捉关键信息，帮助用户轻松回顾会议细节。使用简便，提升会议记录效率。

producthunt.name: Astute
producthunt.tagline: Automate your B2B brand going viral, with new media creators
producthunt.summary_zh: Astute 是一个自动化平台，帮助企业与新媒体创作者合作，快速提升品牌知名度。通过简化品牌宣传流程，企业可以轻松实现内容的病毒式传播。

producthunt.name: Dograh
producthunt.summary_zh: Dograh 是一个开源的 VAPI 替代方案，旨在提供灵活的 API 解决方案。用户可以使用它创建、管理和测试 API，简化开发过程，提高效率。这个工具支持多种编程语言，方便开发者集成。

producthunt.name: Grok Bot
producthunt.tagline: AI teammates that you can give real work to
producthunt.summary_zh: Grok Bot是一款智能助手，可以作为你的工作搭档执行实际任务。它可以处理信息、回答问题和完成日常工作，让你更高效地完成目标。通过与Grok Bot协作，你可以节省时间和精力。

producthunt.name: Memmy Agent
producthunt.tagline: Let every AI remember the same you.
producthunt.summary_zh: Memmy Agent 是一款智能工具，可以让不同的人工智能系统记住你的个性化信息。通过它，你的偏好和特点将被同步到多个AI中，从而提供更加个性化的服务。使用 Memmy Agent，你无需重复输入信息，AI将更好地了解你。

producthunt.name: Adomate
producthunt.tagline: Turn data into winning ads. At scale.
producthunt.summary_zh: Adomate是一款广告自动化工具，能够将数据转化为高效的广告。它帮助用户在大规模上创造和优化广告，提高投放效果。通过智能分析和实时调整，Adomate让广告投放更加精准和省时。

producthunt.name: Coldtea.ai
producthunt.summary_zh: Coldtea.ai 是一款智能软件工具，它可以自动化软件的运行和管理流程。用户只需简单设置，系统就能自主完成复杂任务，提高工作效率。

producthunt.name: AI Search Console
producthunt.tagline: Prompt analytics and citation mapping for AI search
producthunt.summary_zh: AI Search Console 是一款用于分析AI搜索的工具，能帮助用户了解搜索提示的效果和引用的来源。它提供数据分析和可视化图谱，便于优化搜索结果和提高搜索效率。

producthunt.name: Meridian
producthunt.tagline: Don't let your work go unnoticed. Get promoted!
producthunt.summary_zh: Meridian是一款专注于职业发展的工具。它可以帮助用户记录并展示自己的工作成就，让你在职场上获得更多关注和晋升机会。通过使用Meridian，你可以轻松整理和分享自己的工作亮点。

github_trending.description: Agent skill for beautiful, verifiable architecture, workflow, sequence, data-flow, and lifecycle diagrams—self-contained HTML with motion and crisp export.
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目是一个帮助用户创建美观且可验证的建筑、工作流程、序列、数据流和生命周期图表的工具，生成的图表以HTML格式自包含，支持动画效果和清晰的导出。对Yves来说，这个工具可以帮助Logic Labs提升AI项目的可视化表现，同时也能为TexTale的创意设计提供灵感，帮助更好地展现产品和品牌故事。

github_trending.description: Prompt as Code | GPT-Image2 工业级提示词引擎与模板库，530+ 个案例逆向工程，20+ 套工业级模板，并提炼出Skills，持续更新中
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目旨在提供一个工业级的提示词引擎和模板库，帮助用户更有效地生成图像，特别是利用 AI 来提升创意设计的效率。对于Yves来说，这个工具非常适合应用于Logic Labs（AI公司），可以优化AI图像生成的流程并提升创意输出，同时也可以为TexTale的产品设计和营销提供灵感和创意支持。

github_trending.description: Official, Anthropic-managed directory of high quality Claude Code Plugins.
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目是一个官方目录，提供高质量的Claude代码插件，旨在帮助开发者更方便地使用Claude AI模型进行各种任务。对于Yves而言，这个项目可以帮助Logic Labs在AI应用方面提升创意设计的效率，并为其产品开发提供强大的AI工具支持。同时，运用这些插件也有助于TexTale提升电商平台的个性化推荐和用户体验。

github_trending.description: Use Claude Code, Codex, Pi, and OpenCode for free (1.3B+ free tokens) from your terminal, app, IDE, or phone like OpenClaw (voice supported + ToS friendly)
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目提供了一种便捷的方式，让用户可以免费使用 Claude Code、Codex 等 AI 编程工具，通过终端、应用程序或手机进行操作，类似于 OpenClaw，并支持语音输入。对 Yves 来说，这个工具可以帮助 Logic Labs 的 AI 产品开发，加速构思和实现创新设计，提高工作效率，也能在 TexTale 的技术服装电商中提升产品的智能化服务。作为创意设计从业者，这个项目能够激发其创意，拓展设计的可能性。

github_trending.description: The job search that runs on your machine. AI job application framework built on Claude Code: evaluate postings, tailor CVs, write cover letters, prep interviews. Fork it and own it.
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目是一个AI驱动的求职助手，可以帮助用户评估工作岗位、量身定制简历、撰写求职信以及准备面试。对于Yves来说，它可能更有助于Logic Labs，因为他可以利用这个工具高效地寻找并申请与AI相关的创新项目，同时也能够为自身的设计技能积累更多与AI行业相关的体验。

github_trending.description: Self-organizing AI second brain for Obsidian + Claude Code. Drop any source and Claude reads, links, and files it into one connected knowledge graph of plain Markdown you own. AI note-taking, personal knowledge management (PKM), and an open-source Notion alternative. Based on Karpathy's LLM Wiki pattern.
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目是一个自动组织信息的 AI 工具，可以帮助用户在 Obsidian 中创建和管理个人知识库。用户只需将资料投入，Claude 就会自动读取、链接和整理这些信息，形成一个个性化的知识图谱。对于 Yves 来说，这个工具可以帮助他在 Logic Labs 改进 AI 驱动的创意设计过程，提升信息管理效率，同时也为 TexTale 的市场分析和产品创新提供了有价值的洞见。
这个项目旨在提供一个美观、现代且有独特观点的Linux操作系统，适合追求美学与功能性的用户。对Yves而言，这个项目对TexTale（科技服装电商）可能更有帮助，因为它可以提升电商平台的用户体验与界面设计，从而增强品牌形象。同时，作为创意设计从业者，他也能从中获取灵感，为自己的设计工作带来新的视角。

github_trending.description: Learn it. Build it. Ship it for others.
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目是一个全面的教程，教人们如何从零开始学习和构建人工智能应用，最终将其推向市场。对 Yves 的 Logic Labs（AI 公司）特别有帮助，因为可以为他们提供实用的 AI 技能和工具，增强团队的工程能力，从而推动创新。同时，作为创意设计从业者，他也能从中获得灵感，将 AI 应用于设计流程中提升创意效果。

github_trending.description: Your Personal AI super intelligence. A brain that builds a local-first memory of your life, a fantastic orchestrator of agent fleets and workflows, and a deep researcher.
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目是一个个人AI超级智能工具，能够记录和整理你的生活记忆，并高效地管理多个任务和工作流程，甚至可以进行深度研究。对Yves的Logic Labs（AI公司）将特别有帮助，因为它可以为AI产品提供强大的智能支持，优化产品的功能和用户体验，同时也可能为TexTale的电商运营提供个性化的客户服务解决方案。作为创意设计从业者，这个工具有助于提升创意工作的效率和灵感管理。

github_trending.description: Makes your AI agent think like the laziest senior dev in the room. The best code is the code you never wrote.
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目旨在通过模拟懒惰的高级开发者的思维方式，使得AI代理在编写代码时更加高效，达到“最好代码是你从未写过的代码”的目标。对于Yves的Logic Labs，它可以帮助优化AI模型的开发过程，提高项目的研发效率；而对于TexTale来说，运用这一理念可以推动在电商平台上的快捷开发和更智能的系统搭建，从而提升用户体验和运营效率。作为创意设计从业者，Yves可以借助这种工具激发更多创意想法，减轻重复性工作的负担。
